subtitle: Rebel King of Later Baekje
description: Gyeon Hwon (867-936) was the founder and first king of Later Baekje, one of the Later Three Kingdoms of Korea. His life is a blend of historical record and mythological embellishment. Born as a peasant, stories claim his mother conceived after contact with a worm, imbuing him with supernatural origins. He rose to prominence during the waning years of Silla, leading peasant revolts and capitalizing on the kingdom's weakened state. He established Later Baekje in 900, aiming to revive the glory of the ancient Baekje kingdom. His reign was marked by constant warfare against Silla and Later Goguryeo (Taebong), eventually leading to his defeat and exile. Despite his short-lived kingdom, Gyeon Hwon remains a significant figure in Korean history, representing ambition, rebellion, and the complexities of power.

extendedContent.title: Origins & Mythology
extendedContent.content: Gyeon Hwon's origins are steeped in myth. The Samguk Yusa recounts the story of his mother conceiving after an encounter with a worm, suggesting a divine or extraordinary birth. He was born in Sangju, and his rise to power began with his service as a military officer in Silla. Recognizing the kingdom's decline, he gathered followers and led a rebellion, quickly gaining control over key territories. He declared himself king in 900, establishing Later Baekje and claiming descent from the Baekje royal family. His early military successes further solidified his position, but his reign was constantly challenged by the other kingdoms.

extendedContent.title: Role & Significance
extendedContent.content: Gyeon Hwon's role is pivotal in the transition from the Unified Silla period to the Later Three Kingdoms and, ultimately, the Goryeo dynasty. He represented a challenge to the established order and a longing for the past glory of Baekje. His kingdom, though ultimately unsuccessful, played a crucial role in reshaping the political landscape of the Korean peninsula. He is seen as a symbol of ambition and rebellion against a decaying regime, but also as a figure whose actions contributed to a period of intense conflict and instability. He is a reminder of the cyclical nature of power and the enduring appeal of regional identity.

extendedContent.title: Symbolism & Interpretation
extendedContent.content: Gyeon Hwon symbolizes the desire for regional autonomy and the rejection of centralized power. His claim to be a descendant of the Baekje royal family represents a longing for a glorious past and a rejection of Silla's dominance. His military successes and his ability to attract followers symbolize charismatic leadership and the power of rebellion. However, his ultimate failure and exile also symbolize the limitations of ambition and the dangers of unchecked power. His story is often interpreted as a cautionary tale about the complexities of leadership and the importance of strategic alliances.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: Gyeon Hwon's legacy is complex. While his kingdom was short-lived, he remains a significant figure in Korean history and folklore. He is often portrayed in historical dramas and literature as a charismatic but flawed leader. His story continues to resonate with those who admire his ambition and his willingness to challenge the status quo. However, he is also remembered for the violence and instability that characterized his reign. His actions paved the way for the rise of Goryeo, which ultimately unified the Korean peninsula. He is a reminder of the turbulent period of transition and the enduring power of regional identities.
